text: C3 holds up a picture frame with ‘Scene 4’ on the back
speaker: C3

text: Scene 4
speaker: C3

text: C3 turns the frame round to reveal a picture of Lord Henry’s Parlour
speaker: C3

text: Meeting Lady Wotton
speaker: C2/3

text: Lord Henry’s house - somewhere in Mayfair.  Dorian was waiting. Lord Henry has not yet come in.  He was always late on principle.
speaker: C2

text: His principle being that punctuality is the thief of time
speaker: C5

text: At last he heard a step outside, and the door opened.
speaker: C3

text: It was Lady Wotton.  She was a curious woman, whose dresses always looked as if they had been designed in a rage and put on in a tempest.
speaker: Lady W

text: Her name was Victoria and she had a perfect mania for going to church.
speaker: C2

text: (remains with his back to her) How late you are, Harry!
speaker: Dorian

text: I am afraid it is not Harry, Mr. Gray.
speaker: Lady W

text: (turns) I beg your pardon I thought …
speaker: Dorian

text: You thought it was my husband.  It is only his wife.  I know you quite well by your photographs.  I think my husband has got seventeen of them.
speaker: Lady W

text: Not seventeen, Lady Wotton?
speaker: Dorian

text: Well, eighteen, then.  And I saw you with him the other night at the opera.   I like Wagner's music better than anybody's. It is so loud that one can talk the whole time without other people hearing what one says.  That is a great advantage, don't you think so, Mr. Gray?
speaker: Lady W

text: I am afraid I don't think so, Lady Wotton.  I never talk during music - at least, during good music.  If one hears bad music, it is one's duty to drown it in conversation.
speaker: Dorian

text: Ah! that is one of Harry's views, isn't it, Mr.Gray?  I always hear Harry's views from his friends.  It is the only way I get to know of them.
speaker: Lady W

text: But here is Harry! Harry, I came in to look for you, to ask you something - I forget what it was - and I found Mr. Gray here. He has been most pleasant.  I am so glad I've seen him.
speaker: Lady W

text: I am charmed, my love, quite charmed. So sorry I am late, Dorian.  I went to look after a piece of old brocade in Wardour Street and had to bargain for hours for it. Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.
speaker: Lord H

text: I am afraid I must be going I have promised to drive with the duchess.  Good-bye, Mr. Gray.  Good-bye, Harry.  You are dining out, I suppose?  So am I. Perhaps I shall see you at Lady Thornbury’s.
speaker: Lady W

text: Never marry, Dorian.  Men marry because they are tired; women, because they are curious: both are disappointed.
speaker: Lord H

text: I don't think I am likely to marry, Harry. I am too much in love.
speaker: Dorian

text: Who are you in love with?
speaker: Lord H

text: With an actress.
speaker: Dorian

text: That is a rather commonplace debut.
speaker: Lord H

text: You would not say so if you saw her, Harry.
speaker: Dorian

text: Who is she?
speaker: Lord H

text: Her name is Sibyl Vane.
speaker: Dorian

text: Never heard of her.
speaker: Lord H

text: No one has.  People will someday, however.  She is a genius.
speaker: Dorian

text: How long have you known her?
speaker: Lord H

text: About three weeks.
speaker: Dorian

text: And where did you come across her?
speaker: Lord H

text: It never would have happened if I had not met you.  You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. One evening I went in search of adventure.  I went wandered eastward, soon losing my way in a labyrinth of grimy streets. I passed by an absurd little theatre.
speaker: Dorian

text: A hideous man, who appeared to be the manager, was standing at the entrance.  He wore the most amazing waistcoat.
speaker: Manager C1

text: He was smoking a vile cigar.  He had greasy ringlets, and an enormous diamond blazed in the centre of a soiled shirt.
speaker: C3

text: Have a box, my Lord.
speaker: Manager C1

text: There was something about him, Harry, that amused me. You will laugh at me, I know, but I really went in and paid a whole guinea for a private box. I looked out from behind the curtain and surveyed the house.
speaker: Dorian

text: It was a tawdry affair, all Cupids and cornucopias, like a third-rate wedding-cake.
speaker: C4

text: The gallery and pit were fairly full, but there was hardly a person in what I suppose they called the dress-circle.
speaker: C1

text: Women went about with oranges and ginger-beer, and there was a terrible consumption of nuts going on.  The play was Romeo and Juliet.  There was a dreadful orchestra, presided over by a young man who sat at a cracked piano,
speaker: C2

text: Romeo was a stout elderly gentleman, with corked eyebrows, a husky tragedy voice, and a figure like a beer-barrel.
speaker: C4

text: Mercutio was almost as bad.  He was played by the low-comedian, who had introduced gags of his own and was on most friendly terms with the pit.
speaker: C1

text: But Juliet!  Harry, imagine….
speaker: Dorian

text: a girl hardly seventeen years of age, with a little, flowerlike face, a small Greek head with plaited coils of dark-brown hair, eyes that were violet wells of passion, lips that were like the petals of a rose.
speaker: Sibyl

text: She was the loveliest thing I had ever seen in my life.   And her voice - it was very low at first, with deep mellow notes
speaker: Dorian

text: Go ask his name: if he be married My grave is like to be my wedding bed.
speaker: Sibyl

text: Then it became more passionate like a flute
speaker: Dorian

text: My only love sprung from my only hate! Too early seen unknown, and known too late! Prodigious birth of love it is to me, That I must love a loathed enemy
speaker: Sibyl

text: In the garden-scene it had all the tremulous ecstasy that one hears when nightingales are singing.
speaker: Dorian

text: O Romeo, Romeo! Wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse his name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.
speaker: Sibyl

text: There were moments, later on, when it had the wild passion of violins.
speaker: Dorian

text: O, swear not by the moon, the innocent moon, That monthly changes in her cycled orb, Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
speaker: Sibyl

text: Your voice and the voice of Sibyl Vane are two things that I shall never forget and each of them says something different.  I don't know which to follow.  Why should I not love her?  She is everything to me in life.  Night after night I go to see her play.  One evening she is Rosalind, and the next she is Imogen.  I have seen her die, sucking the poison from her lover's lips.  I have watched her disguised as a pretty boy. She has been mad, and she has been innocent. Ordinary women never appeal to one's imagination. How different an actress is!  Harry! why didn't you tell me that the only thing worth loving is an actress?
speaker: Dorian

text: Because I have loved so many of them, Dorian.
speaker: Lord H

text: I wish now I had not told you about Sibyl Vane.
speaker: Dorian

text: You could not have helped telling me, Dorian. All through your life you will tell me everything you do.
speaker: Lord H

text: Yes, Harry, I believe that is true.  I cannot help telling you things. You have a curious influence over me.  If I ever did a crime, I would come and confess it to you.  You would understand me.
speaker: Dorian

text: People like you don't commit crimes, Dorian. Now tell me what are your actual relations with Sibyl Vane? When did you first speak to her?
speaker: Lord H

text: The third night   She had been playing Rosalind.  I could not help going round.  I had thrown her some flowers, and she had looked at me.  Oh, she was so shy and so gentle. There is something of a child about her.   I think we were both rather nervous.
speaker: Dorian

text: (C2 moves frame into place) The old manager stood grinning in the doorway of the dusty green room.
speaker: C2

text: He would insist on calling me 'My Lord,' so I had to assure Sibyl that I was not anything of the kind.
speaker: Dorian

text: You look more like a prince.  I must call you Prince Charming.
speaker: Sibyl

text: Miss Sibyl knows how to pay compliments.
speaker: Lord H

text: You don't understand her, Harry. She knows nothing of life. She lives with her mother, a faded tired woman who played Lady Capulet on the first night, and looks as if she had seen better days.
speaker: Dorian

text: (examining his rings) I know that look.  It depresses me. You can dine with me to-night, Dorian, can't you?
speaker: Lord H

text: Not tonight. To-night she is Imogen and to-morrow night she will be Juliet.
speaker: Dorian

text: When is she Sibyl Vane?
speaker: Lord H

text: Never.
speaker: Dorian

text: I congratulate you.
speaker: Lord H

text: I want you and Basil to come with me some night and see her act. Then we must get her out of the manager’s hands. She is bound to him for three years.  I shall have to pay him something, of course.  When all that is settled, I shall take a West End theatre and bring her out properly.
speaker: Dorian

text: Well, what night shall we go?
speaker: Lord H

text: Let us fix tomorrow. She plays Juliet tomorrow.
speaker: Dorian

text: All right.  The Bristol at eight o'clock and I will get Basil.
speaker: Lord H

text: Dear Basil!  I have not laid eyes on him for a week.  It is rather horrid of me, as he has sent me my portrait in the most wonderful frame, specially designed by himself. Basil is the best of fellows, but he seems to me to be just a bit of a Philistine.  Since I have known you, Harry, I have discovered that.  And now I am off. Imogen is waiting for me.  Don't forget about to-morrow. Good-bye. (he exits)
speaker: Dorian

text: Lord Henry watched him go.
speaker: Lord H

text: He was conscious that it was through certain words of his, that Dorian Gray's soul had turned to this girl and bowed in worship before her
speaker: C2

text: Later, when he arrived home after a visit to his club, he saw a telegram lying on the hall table.
speaker: C4

text: He opened it and found it was from Dorian Gray.  It was to tell him that he was engaged to be married to Sibyl Vane.
speaker: C1
